message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
This paper proposes raising three main-course prices from 1 April and replacing the mushroom risotto with a seasonal vegetarian special. It projects £42,000 a year in extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%.

The price rises themselves are reasonable: all three stay below the competitor midpoints, which checks out. But the paper gets the risotto backwards, leaves out the beef cost rise it reports in §4, and appears to calculate margins on prices that include VAT. Corrected, the price rises add roughly **£20,000–23,000 a year**, about half the figure claimed. The risotto change would *lower* the margin.

## 1. The risotto has the strongest margin, not the weakest

- Its margin is **80%** (£2.80 food cost on £14.00), the highest on the menu. Steak is the weakest at 60%.
- Its sales of 90 a week are joint lowest, tied with specials.
- Specials run at **64%** margin. Replacing the risotto with a special at the same price would add about **£200 a week in food cost**, assuming a typical special margin.
- The risotto appears to be the **only vegetarian main**. Groups that include a vegetarian often choose where to eat based on that, so the dish may bring in tables worth more than its own 90 plates.

The author's description repeats the error ("weakest margin on the menu").

## 2. The beef cost rise is left out of the projection

- §4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. §5.3 assumes food costs stay the same.
- **Steak:** £10.40 × 12% ≈ **+£1.25 a plate**. That uses up most of the £2.00 rise, which comes to £1.67 once VAT is removed (see §3).
- **Burger:** beef is part of the £4.20 cost, so roughly **+£0.30–0.50 a plate**.
- Together that's about **£230–280 a week** missing from the projection.

## 3. The figures appear to include VAT

UK menu prices must include 20% VAT, and gross margin is normally calculated on the price *excluding* VAT. Table 1's margins and the £810 a week both seem to use VAT-inclusive prices.

- A £1.00 menu increase brings in **£0.83** of revenue. The £810 a week becomes **£675**.
- Actual margins are lower than Table 1 shows. Fish and chips is about **63%**, not 69%.

The two corrections together:

| Dish | Extra revenue per plate (excl. VAT) | Extra beef cost per plate | Net gain per plate | Plates/week | £/week |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £0.83 | — | £0.83 | 310 | £258 |
| Burger | £0.83 | £0.30–0.50 | £0.33–0.53 | 260 | £87–139 |
| Steak | £1.67 | £1.25 | £0.42 | 120 | £50 |
| **Total** | | | | | **£395–447** |

That's about **£20,500–23,200 a year**, before any loss of sales.

Once the beef cost rise and the risotto swap are included, main-course margin stays roughly where it is now, not up to 71%. The paper's own figures, which include VAT, put the current margin at about 70%.

## 4. The volume assumption is fragile

Losing just a few plates a week would cancel the gains:

| Dish | Sales drop that cancels the gain |
|---|---|
| Fish and chips | about 9% |
| Burger | about 4–6% |
| Steak | about 3–4% |

- **The steak rise barely covers the beef cost.** Losing four or five steaks a week cancels it.
- **Loyal customers aren't necessarily less price-sensitive.** Regulars are the guests most likely to notice a price change.
- **"No visible effect" in 2024** is an observation, not a measured result.
- **Weekday lunch isn't shown to be "a small share."** Friday and Saturday dinner make up just under half of sales, so the other half includes every lunch plus Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday dinners.

## 5. The monitoring plan would miss a drop in sales

Comparing April and May against **January and February** will almost certainly show sales *rising*, because January and February are usually the quietest months of the year. Even a real loss of customers could look like growth. Better comparisons:
- the same weeks in 2025, or
- each dish's share of total mains, or plates per cover, which seasonal swings affect much less.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** §2 says Wednesday to Sunday (five days); §8 says "six trading days a week."
- **Fish prices** are described as volatile, and fish and chips is the biggest seller. A fish price spike would hit the largest single gain in the projection.
- **The annual figure** assumes 52 trading weeks. Any closure weeks should be deducted.

## A stronger version of the proposal

1. **Keep the risotto.** It's the most profitable dish per pound of sales and probably the only vegetarian main. If the menu needs a seasonal vegetarian option, add it alongside.
2. **Keep the fish and chips and burger rises.** They're well supported.
3. **Revisit the steak price.** At £28.00 it barely absorbs the beef increase. £28.50–29.00 is still below the competitor midpoint of £29.50.
4. **Restate the projection** excluding VAT and including the new beef costs, with a version that assumes sales fall by 5%.
5. **Monitor against the same weeks last year**, and track plates per cover.

With those changes, the review would show a real but more modest gain of about £20,000 a year, and it would avoid removing the menu's highest-margin dish.
